name: Creating a List that Contains the Numbers of Times Each Element of One List Appears in Another List
description: Construct a program that has a function that receives two lists and creates a list that contains the number of times each element in the 2nd list appears in the 1st list. For example, if the 1st list is [1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5, 6] and the 2nd list is [3, 4, 5, 6, 7], then the list that contains the number of times each element in the 2nd list appears in the 1st list is [2, 2, 1, 1, 0].\nAssume that all elements in the 2nd list are unique.
code:
#Step 1: Define the function 
def search_lists(lst1, lst2):
    #Step 1.1: Create a list that we need to store the number of matches
    counts = [0] * len(lst2)
    #Step 1.2: Iterate through the values in the 2nd list
    for val2 in lst2:
        #Step 1.2.1: Iterate through the values in the 1st list
        for val1 in lst1:
            #Step 1.2.1.1: Increment the number of matches for val2 if we find a match for that
            if val2 == val1: 
                counts[ lst2.index(val2) ] += 1
    print("The list that contains the number of times each element in the 2nd list appears in the 1st list:", counts)
#Step 2: Call the function
values_1 = [2.0, 11, 11, 4, 5, 3, 3, 3.5, 4, 10, 16]
values_2 =  [7, 11, 3]
search_lists(values_1, values_2)

commentList:
We need to first declare the function so that we can call it later. The following lines declares the function search_lists that takes two lists and creates a list that contains the the number of times each element in the 2nd list appears in the 1st list.

Note that all statements following the header line are indented.

3.content: #Step 1.1: Create a list that we need to store the number of matches

commentList: We need N variables to store the number of matches for each element in the 2nd list; that means a list is a great way to store this data. Therefore, we need to create a list with the same length as the 2nd list and fill it with 0s as we have not started counting yet. In general, the element at index i in this list will be used for storing the number of times the element at index i in the 2nd list appears in the 1st list.
The repetition operator * makes N copies of the list [0] and joins them all together into a single list, where N is the number of elements in the 2nd list.

Note that the function len(lst2) returns the number of elements in the 2nd list. Also, note that when the operand on the left side of the * is a list, it becomes the repetition operator and not the multiplication.

5.content: #Step 1.2: Iterate through the values in the 2nd list

commentList: We want to iterate through the 2nd list and count how many times each element of 2nd list appears in the 1st list. We iterate through the 2nd list using for loop because for loop can step across any kind of sequence object including lists.
This for loop assigns the name val2 to each of the elements in the 2nd list in turn, from left to right, and then the statements in the loop body will be executed for each.

7.content: #Step 1.2.1: Iterate through the values in the 1st list

commentList: We need to iterate through the 1st list and count how many times the value that we visited in the 2nd list (val2) appears in the 1st list. We iterate through the 1st list using for loop because for loop can step across any kind of sequence object including lists.
This for loop assigns the name val1 to each of the values in the 1st list in turn, from left to right, and then the statements in the loop body will be executed for each.

9.content: #Step 1.2.1.1: Increment the number of matches for val2 if we find a match for that

commentList: We check for match between the val1 and val2 using the == operator.
If the visited value in the 2nd list (val2) matches the visited values in the 1st list (val1), then the body of this if statement gets executed. Otherwise, the body of this if statement is skipped.

This statement increments the number of matches for val2 (the value that we visited in the 2nd list) by 1 every time we find a match between val2 and a value in the 1st list.

To update the number of matches that corresponds to val2, we need to find the index in the counts that corresponds to val2. When we find the index, we increment the value that is stored at that index by 1.

The index function returns the lowest index in 2nd list that val2 appears. Since all elements of the 2nd list are unique, each value in the 2nd list appears in only one index; and thus, we always get the right index for val2.

When the returned index is i, we increment the number of matches for the value at index i in the 2nd list.
Note that we do not necessarily have to store the returned value from the index function in a variable. We could use the index function call directly as the list index.

Note that the += operator adds 1 to the value stored in counts[lst2.index(val2)] and the result is stored into the element counts[lst2.index(val2)]. Therefore, it is functionally equivalent to the statement counts[lst2.index(val2)] = counts[lst2.index(val2)] + 1.
